result_expr: Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), t) + M*(6*gamma/eps*phi(x, y, z, t)*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))*(1 - 2*phi(x, y, z, t)) - 6*gamma*eps*(Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (x, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (y, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (z, 2)))) - alpha*30*phi(x, y, z, t)**2*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))**2*(rho_v(x, y, z, t) - rho_vs(T(x, y, z, t)))

symbols.name: M
symbols.meaning: interface mobility (Allen-Cahn kinetic coefficient): how fast $\phi$ relaxes down the gradient of $F$; with it a curved interface moves at $v_n=-6\gamma\varepsilon M\kappa$

symbols.name: alpha
symbols.meaning: deposition/sublimation rate coefficient; a flat interface advances into the gas at $v_n = 6\varepsilon\alpha(\rho_v-\rho_{vs})$, so $6\varepsilon\alpha = k/\rho_i$ with $k$ a kinetic mass-transfer velocity (Hertz-Knudsen: $k=a_s\sqrt{k_BT/2\pi m}$) and $\rho_i$ the ice density

symbols.name: p(phi)
symbols.meaning: interface-localizing function $30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, zero in bulk ice and gas, $\int_0^1 p\,d\phi = 1$

symbols.name: phi_0(n)
symbols.meaning: equilibrium flat-interface profile along the normal coordinate $n$

symbols.name: n
symbols.meaning: coordinate normal to a flat interface, pointing into the ice

symbols.name: v_n
symbols.meaning: normal velocity of the interface, positive when ice grows

symbols.name: kappa
symbols.meaning: sum of principal curvatures of the interface (positive for a convex ice grain)

steps.title: Variational derivative of F
steps.why: The interface relaxes down the gradient of $F$, so we need $\delta F/\delta\phi$. The Euler-Lagrange operator applied to the integrand gives it; the boundary term is dropped with no-flux (natural) boundary conditions.
steps.operation: Euler-Lagrange derivative of the integrand of F

steps.title: Relaxation part (Allen-Cahn)
steps.why: $\phi$ is not conserved (ice turns into vapor), so the simplest relaxation that always lowers $F$ is the non-conserved gradient flow, with a positive mobility $M$. Then $dF/dt=-\int M\mu^2\,dV\le 0$.

check.printed: Constitutive choice; units checked in check_units: M*gam/eps -> 1/s.

steps.title: Phase-change source term
steps.why: Deposition must raise $\phi$ where $\rho_v>\rho_{vs}(T)$ and lower it where $\rho_v<\rho_{vs}$, to linear order in the departure. With no nucleation the source must vanish in pure gas and pure ice, so we multiply by $p(\phi)=30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, which is zero at $\phi=0,1$ with zero slope there (bulk phases stay fixed points) and is normalized to $\int_0^1p\,d\phi=1$.
steps.operation: postulate linear driving term localized to the interface

steps.title: Evolution equation
steps.why: The two mechanisms act in parallel, so their rates add. Moving everything to one side gives the residual $R$.
steps.operation: add S2 and S3, substitute S1, move to left side

steps.title: Flat equilibrium profile is consistent with A2
steps.why: To read off what $M$ and $\alpha$ mean, we need the flat profile with $\mu=0$. The logistic profile solves it, has 10-90% width $2\ln 9\,\varepsilon$ and energy $\gamma$ per area, as A2 states.

check.printed: profile solves dF/dphi=0: True; 10-90 width: 4*epsilon*log(3); energy per area: gamma; int phi0_n^2 dn: 1/(6*epsilon)

steps.title: Meaning of the coefficients
steps.why: Put a front $\phi=\phi_0(n+v_nt)$ into S4, multiply by $\phi_0'$ and integrate across the interface; the $\mu$ term vanishes for the flat profile, and the Laplacian term gives the usual Allen-Cahn curvature law. This shows that $\alpha$ sets the deposition speed and $M$ sets the curvature-driven (Gibbs-Thomson-like) motion.
steps.operation: solvability: multiply by phi_0' and integrate over n

check.printed: S6 V = [6*Delta*alpha*epsilon]; diffusion coefficient on laplacian: 6*M*epsilon*gamma

assumptions_used: A1 (given): $\rho_v$ and $T$ are known, smooth fields.
A2 (given): the flat interface described by $F$ has energy $\gamma$ per unit area and a 10-90 % width of $2\ln 9\,\varepsilon$.

A3: Near equilibrium, the interface relaxes by linear, non-conserved (Allen-Cahn) gradient flow $\partial_t\phi=-M\,\delta F/\delta\phi$ with a positive scalar mobility $M$ (isotropic, taken constant).
A4: The growth rate depends linearly on the supersaturation $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}(T)$ (linear kinetics, as in Hertz-Knudsen), with a constant positive coefficient $\alpha$.

A5: No nucleation: the source is multiplied by $p(\phi)=30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, which is zero in bulk ice and gas, so ice changes only at the existing interface. Any other localized $p$ with $\int_0^1 p\,d\phi=1$ would give the same sharp-interface limit.
A6: Relaxation and phase change act in parallel, so their rates add.

neglected.effect: Anisotropy of ice surface energy and kinetics (faceting)
neglected.why: Taken as isotropic: $\gamma$, $M$ and $\alpha$ are scalars. This is acceptable for rounded pore-scale grains; anisotropy would add orientation-dependent factors.
Kept constant for simplicity. Their Arrhenius or $\sqrt{T}$ variation can be restored by writing $M(T)$ and $\alpha(T)$ without changing the form of the equation.
The pore vapor is close to saturation ($|\rho_v-\rho_{vs}|/\rho_{vs}\ll1$), so the linear term is the leading order and the dropped terms are $O((\Delta/\rho_{vs})^2)$.

neglected.effect: Curvature dependence of the saturation density (explicit Gibbs-Thomson term in $\rho_{vs}$)
neglected.why: It is represented by the $M$-term ($v_n\propto-\kappa$). Matching $6\gamma\varepsilon M=6\varepsilon\alpha\rho_{vs}\gamma/(\rho_i R_vT)\cdot$(molar factors) would make it quantitative; that choice is left to the calibration of $M$. The size is $\rho_{vs}\gamma/(\rho_iR_vT\,r)\sim10^{-4}\rho_{vs}$ for $r\sim1\,\mu$m.

neglected.effect: Mechanical stress, elasticity and grain motion of ice and regolith
neglected.why: The regolith grains and ice are treated as rigid; stresses are outside this model.
Deterministic model; noise is needed only for nucleation, which is excluded.

neglected.effect: Wetting of regolith grains by ice (contact angle at grain walls)
neglected.why: Boundary conditions at the grain surfaces are taken as natural (no-flux), as needed to drop the boundary term in S1; a wetting energy would add a surface term.

questions: The interface function $p(\phi)=30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$ is my choice. Any localized $p$ with $\int_0^1p\,d\phi=1$ gives the same sharp-interface speed. If your model uses a different one, such as $\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$ without the 30, $\alpha$ has to be rescaled to match.
Should $M$ be tied to $\alpha$ through the Gibbs-Thomson relation, so that curvature-driven sublimation agrees with the Kelvin equation? Or should it stay a free parameter?
